title: Diogenes throws away his cup
hook: seeing a child drink from cupped hands, he tosses away his last possession

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes and the king: stand out of my light, because some good things are already shining. Today closes week five.
screen: `DIOGENES AND THE KING — STAND OUT OF MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Somewhere near you there's a junk drawer. Old chargers for phones nobody owns anymore. Keys to nothing. A takeout menu from a place that closed. Now meet a man whose whole house fits in a small bag over his shoulder: a cloak, a stick, a bag, and a cup for drinking. That's Diogenes, the Cynic who told Alexander to move out of his sunlight. One day he watched a child get a drink of water, and lost one more thing.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF KEYS TO NOTHING.` → `A CLOAK, A STICK, A BAG, A CUP.` → `A CHILD, DRINKING.`

segments.voice: Diogenes Laërtius tells it like this. Diogenes sees a child drinking water from his cupped hands. He pulls the cup out of his bag and throws it away, saying something like: a child has beaten me at living simply. The same source tells a twin story: seeing a boy who'd broken his bowl eat lentils from a hollowed piece of bread, he threw away his bowl too. Notice who the teacher is. Not a philosopher: a child, someone who didn't know you're supposed to need a cup. The man who owned almost nothing still found something to put down. Careful, though. This is a story about choosing to carry less, not one that makes poverty romantic. Diogenes chose his life, and plenty of people in his world, and ours, don't get to choose. The Cynics weren't after hardship for its own sake. They were after freedom. One way to put their point: every thing you own also owns a little of you. It needs storing, protecting, repairing, worrying about. Put it down and your hands are free. That closes week five: Rome's hard nights, Cato, Seneca on a life long enough, his consolatio to his mother from exile, imago vitae in his last hours, Diogenes in the sun, and a cup thrown away because a child knew better. Hard stories, most of them, each asking the same quiet question: when everything else is taken, or given away, what's left? Tomorrow, a new week, and a very different teacher: a wise fool.
screen: `A CHILD DRINKS FROM HIS HANDS.` · `THE TEACHER IS A CHILD.` · `CHOSEN, NOT ROMANTIC.` · `WEEK FIVE: WHAT'S LEFT?` · then, large: `LESS TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Take a slow tour of your home in your mind: the closet, the drawers, the shelf you never look at. Find one thing you don't use and wouldn't miss, something someone else could use, and picture handing it to them. Then notice how your hands feel.
Diogenes, the man who owned almost nothing and still found one more thing to put down, after a child beat him at living simply.
Your line: less to carry. Seven stories of hard nights and open hands. Week five, done.

screen: `DAY 35 COUNTS. WEEK FIVE DONE.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING UNDER THE LAMP.`

howItsDone: Many traditions practice voluntary simplicity, from the Cynics and monastic vows of poverty to modern decluttering, giving away what isn't needed so that it can serve someone else.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes. you own a cloak, a stick, a bag and a cup. you watch a child drink water from cupped hands. what do you do?
options: keep the cup. you need something.
fork.reveal: he throws it away, saying a child has beaten him at living simply. later, seeing a boy eat lentils from bread, he throws away his bowl too.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who didn't want a cup.
what it means: even with almost nothing, there's one more thing to put down, and a child can be the teacher.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 6.37 tells both the cup and the bowl; Cynic self-sufficiency was called autarkeia, needing as little as possible.
recall: a Persian Muslim poet and scholar

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.37

notes: DL 6.37: cup thrown from his wallet on seeing a child drink from his hands ('A child has beaten me in plainness of living', paraphrased); bowl thrown away on seeing a boy who had broken his dish eat lentils from a hollow loaf. Confirm.
Diogenes's possessions (cloak, staff, wallet/bag, cup) are the traditional Cynic kit (DL 6.22–23); confirm.
Autarkeia (self-sufficiency) as the Cynic ideal; confirm the trapdoor note.
Week-five look-back in the teach and carry; the teach ends by pointing to week six (Nasruddin).
